notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa005.opp-l: Head: 'FULGENTO' is evidently a scanning error; the title is rendered as 'On the Incarnation... and on the Creator (auctore) of Lowly Animals'. §2: 'subvertis' ('you overturn') makes little sense and is taken as 'subjungis' ('you add'). 'et tu ei ad praesens locutus ea' is corrupt (probably 'locutus es'); the rendering is tentative. 'reddenda nunc ut' is read as 'reddenda nunc est', and 'qua Unita' as 'qua finita'. §4: 'Quid si tamen propriis personae monstrantur' is read as 'Quae si tamen propriis personae monstrantur'; the sentence is syntactically difficult and the rendering is approximate.

§7: the edition's 'in alia (forte illa) missione' is translated with the suggested reading 'illa'. §10: 'nec dominis quemquam posse servire, nec diis' presumably means several lords or gods; 'several' is supplied.

In §12 'Ille ... cognoscitur diligere' the edition suggests 'illum' for 'ille'; translated with that sense ('he is known to love the Father and the Son'). The edition's references 'Hebr. II, 46' and 'Rom. VIII, 52' are scanning errors for Heb. 2:16 and Rom. 8:32; 'Gal. I, 5' covers Gal. 1:3–5. In §15 'Magnæ absurditatis es' is read as 'est'.

In 19 the quotation from Baruch is attributed to Jeremiah, following the traditional association of Baruch with Jeremiah. In 18 'interpretamur' is read as 'interpretatur' ('is interpreted'). Fulgentius's scriptural references follow the Vulgate numbering (e.g. Ps. 17:32 = Ps. 18:31 in Hebrew numbering).

§21: 'mandatum' rendered 'command', playing on 'mandavit' just before. §23 is numbered '25' in the scanned text; read as 23. In §20 the edition's references (John 5:36; 14:15; 15:16) are given as the fuller or corrected ranges (5:36–37; 14:15–17; 15:26).

27: '(al. Et adhuc)' and '(forte Cum)' are editorial variants; 'Eadem' and 'Cum' followed. 26: 'naturae IMMUS' read as 'naturae unius'; 'incomprehensibilis aestas' read as 'incomprehensibilis aeternitatis' (a guess from a garbled scan). 28: the edition marks the text as corrupt at 'quæ cum multum non sivit esse...'; the rendering of that clause is tentative, and 'famulis' is taken as 'flagellis' following the editor's suggestion. 'par- Ii ITI' read as 'partium'. 29: the paragraph ends with a broken 'facit a.'; the sentence about Zacharias is incomplete (perhaps '[recta] facit'), and the reference is unclear. 30: 'ignis acei' read as 'ignis sacer' ('sacred fire', probably erysipelas or a similar inflammation); 'quam venenoso aculeo' read as 'cum...', following the editor; 'misericordia suas' read as 'misericordias suas' (Ps. 76:10).

31: the sentence 'quibus dum naturale dicitur ... reponit' is obscure and probably corrupt; 'reponit' may stand for 'reperit' (finds), which is how it is rendered, and the subject '[harm]' is supplied. 'Species' in the opening sentence is taken in its late sense of a drug or ingredient. 33: 'enicitur' is read as 'efficitur'. 'per habitum et privationem' renders the logical terms of possession and privation.

Section 37: 'capitaliter peccantes' rendered 'sinning mortally'. The edition prints Jamnes et Mambres for the magicians, rendered Jannes and Jambres. Section 43 is misnumbered '45' in the scan. In 44, 'Debm (forte Deo)' read as Deo. Scripture references corrected for evident scanning errors (e.g. Matt. 14:31, Deut. 1:37, 1 Cor. 11:31-32, 1 Pet. 4:17-18).

48: Fulgentius cites Ps. 46:10 as 'XLVI, 18'; reference kept in standard form. 46: 'Marc. xit, 22' read as Mark 13:22. 50: the text has 'ad concupiscendum eum' alongside 'moechatus est eam'; 'eum' is evidently a slip for 'eam'.

51: 'Sed cum bonis recte credens' is awkward and possibly corrupt; translated as 'since one who believes rightly' with 'bonis' taken as anticipating 'angelis bonis'. 'qui in vermibus…sensus' read as 'quia'. 55: 'Non ibi cruciatibus solatia miscebuntur, latiis inserentur' is defective; probably something like 'nec cruciatus solatiis inserentur' has dropped out, restored in brackets. 56: the stray 'natne.' before 'laudandi' appears to be a scanning error and is omitted. The psalm quoted ('Beati qui habitant…') is Ps. 83:5 (Vulgate), though cited as LXXXV.

nodes.text: 8. On the Incarnation of the Son of God and on the Creator of Lowly Animals, to Scarila: one book.

1. Having read the letter you sent, dearest son Scarila, I rejoiced in the Lord, and my soul exulted in God my Saviour, because [he] has clothed you with zeal for salvation and has mercifully poured into your heart a desire for righteousness, by which you long to know the true faith. For through this [faith] the bounty of life comes to human beings, as God himself testified through the prophet, saying: But the righteous lives by faith (Rom. 1:17). That faith, however, must be called true which is true, not feigned, the faith which the holy Apostle commends, saying: But the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned (1 Tim. 1:5). For since the same blessed Paul says that we have been saved by grace through faith, which he declares is not from ourselves but the gift of God (Eph. 2:8), there will certainly be no true salvation where there has been no true faith. When this [faith] is poured in from God, it is without doubt given by free bounty; and where through true faith there is truth of belief, truth of salvation will certainly accompany it. But whoever strays from the true faith will not have the grace of true salvation. Therefore the faithful mind ought not to be sluggish in inquiring, if it sees anything doubtful to itself in the sacrament of faith, above all in the mystery of the Lord's Incarnation, through which righteousness has been given to the ungodly, life to the dead, salvation to the sick, and the grace of true freedom to captives.

2. You wrote, then, to use your own words, that while at the table of my son Eventus, a Christian of the Catholic Church, a conversation arose about the Incarnation of God, one of you asserted this about the Incarnation itself: that it was not God the Father who put on flesh, but only the Son of God. And another said: God himself, who is one in three, deigned to take on flesh, in order to lead to freedom our servitude, in which we were held bound through the transgression of our father Adam. Then you say that you wish to know whether God the Father himself came down and took on flesh, or whether, remaining where he was, he commanded the Word to take on flesh. You say that we also know that the Word was made flesh, so that he might dwell in us. Here you also add these words, saying: But between the Word, who is God, and the Father, who is God, the one majesty of both came down to put on flesh, because, you say, we read: "This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him: after this he was seen on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3:36)." You add further and say that when you brought this testimony forward, that man said on the contrary: He said this of the Son, and not of the Father; and you spoke to him for the moment to the effect that you should have recourse to us about what you were both equally ignorant of. To this question, which the first part of your letter contains, an answer must now be given by us, God granting and helping; and when it is finished, it will not be irksome to answer the other also, as far as God grants.

3. First of all, then, every Catholic Christian ought to know that the holy Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, is one God; and that the Trinity itself, which is one God, is indeed one nature, yet not one person. For what is said, that the one God is the Trinity, is true; for the one God is the Trinity, since the Father does not have one nature, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, but the Trinity itself, God, is one nature. Yet the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not one person; rather, the person of the Father belongs to the Father alone, the person of the Son belongs to the Son alone, and the person of the Holy Spirit belongs to the Holy Spirit alone. Personally, therefore, he who is the Father is not himself the Son, and he who is the Son is not himself the Holy Spirit. But what the Father is by nature, this the Son is, this the Holy Spirit is, because by nature the Trinity itself is one God; where greater and lesser are not spoken of, since no one is found to be earlier or later than another. There the eternity and immensity of each single person is as great as that of the three persons by nature. Yet it is the Father alone who begot the Son; the Son alone who was born of the Father; and the Holy Spirit alone who was neither born of the Father nor begot the Son, but proceeded from the Father and the Son. The Father, therefore, is Father of the Son alone, and the Son is Son of the Father alone; but the Holy Spirit is not of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, but is one and common to the Father and the Son together.

4. In this Trinity, then, there are certain properties of the individual persons. These, however, show the persons by their properties but do not separate them, whose nature, while they are inseparable, cannot be confused; rather, single properties remain in the single persons to this end, that it may show both the natural unity of the true Trinity and the personal Trinity of the true unity. It is proper, therefore, to the Father alone that he himself was not born but begot; it is proper to the Son that he himself did not beget but was born; and it is proper to the Holy Spirit that he himself neither begot nor was born, but proceeds from the begetter and the begotten. And just as the generation by the Father is eternal without beginning, and the birth of the Son is eternal without beginning, so by nature the procession of the Holy Spirit is eternal without beginning. For from the eternity of God the Father, which abides without beginning, the birth of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit are certainly such that both that birth and that procession are coeternal with that origin in which no beginning could in any way be found. Since, therefore, that natural unity of the Trinity has this in itself, that to be born is proper to the Son alone, he [is the one] who alone has in himself the true birth of humanity from the Virgin; for it belonged to him according to the flesh to have truly and by nature a mother, who according to the divinity has truly and by nature a Father. Accordingly, he who was begotten without beginning of the eternal Father is the same who was born in time of a mother in time; and for this reason he is truly called the only-begotten Son of God not only in his divinity but also in the flesh, since both according to the divinity and according to the flesh he alone is found to be begotten.

5. Both births, then, are proper to the only-begotten [Son] of God alone: the one, namely, from the truth of the divine nature, the other from the grace of the humanity assumed. For this reason the evangelist John declares the only-begotten from the Father to be full of grace and truth (John 1:14). Therefore one must beware of that deadly and wholly diabolical blasphemy by which it is believed or said that the Trinity itself together took on flesh, which the Catholic faith does not accept, but which the wickedness of the Sabellian error devised. For Sabellius, who learned that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are proclaimed not three gods but one true God, heard what is true in such a way that he generated for himself what is false. In short, since he learned that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one nature in such a way that he did not hesitate to proclaim one person of the same nature, he was hurled by the madness of his error to the point of asserting that the Father himself was born of the Virgin. And it followed of necessity that to the one to whom he gave the reality of human birth he should also assign the reality of suffering and death. Hence the Catholic Church named the followers of this Sabellius not only Sabellians but also Patripassians, and condemned them with the bond of anathema together with their founder.

6. Far be this perversity, then, from the faithful; and may God not permit anyone redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son to be profaned by this deadly notion of unbelief. For it is great impiety if anyone, regarding the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, either wishes one person to be proclaimed on account of the one nature, or asserts three natures on account of the three persons. Since he who asserts one person of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is caught in the snare of the Sabellian error; while he who affirms that there are three natures of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is bound in the knots of Arian unbelief. And although the assertion of each unbelief seems different, yet the condemnation of both impieties is one. For impiously is the property of the persons confused on account of the unity of nature; and no less impiously is the natural unity separated on account of the persons themselves. The Father has one true Son by nature, born both from himself without beginning and from the Virgin in time. Him he sent into the world, so that the world might be saved through him. The same Son, showing this, says: For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world may be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God (John 3:16-18).

7. See, in this place our Saviour himself calls himself Son three times, and twice named [himself] only-begotten, and asserted that he had been sent by the Father to save the world; whereas certainly, if the Trinity itself had come together in the flesh, the Son would not have said that he was sent by the Father. But Christ could not lie: without doubt one in person sent, and another was sent. And the true Father sent the Truth whom he begot; he sent the Wisdom in which he made all things; he sent the Word which he uttered from his heart. Accordingly, in that sending the coming is not to be reckoned as local, as though the Son of God had been sent from heaven to earth, so that either he was not on earth before he received flesh, or he deserted heaven when he took up flesh for our salvation. Since, then, he himself is the Wisdom of God, of whom it is said: She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), that divinity, which by nature is one of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, is not in place, just as it is not in time; it is not enclosed by place, just as it is not varied by time. That divinity which by nature is immeasurable and eternal neither began with a beginning nor is enclosed by place. Therefore the one God himself, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, fills the whole, contains the whole: thus whole in each, thus whole in all, thus whole in the small, thus whole in the greatest creatures; so by nature, but not so by grace; so when he creates men, not so when he saves [them]; so when he makes, not so when he remakes; so when he makes this sun rise on the good and the evil, not so when the Sun of righteousness rises for those into whom life, not of the flesh but of the heart, is poured by the gift of prevenient mercy. For it does not belong to all to be reborn through grace as it belongs to all to be born through nature. Since, therefore, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are by nature one God, eternal and immeasurable, there is nothing in heaven, nothing on earth, nothing above heaven, nothing in any nature which the unmade God made, where the same one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, could be absent; in whom, just as there is no changeableness of times, so there is no containment by places. This Solomon is found to have said truly at the dedication, in these words: For if heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built (1 Kings 8:27).

8. So God, ineffable and wholly wonderful, ineffably and wonderfully, by the very nature of his immensity, is both whole in each thing and not enclosed by all things together. So is the Father alone, so the Son alone, so the Holy Spirit alone, so together the Trinity, one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: for neither is the Father alone without the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit alone without the Father or the Son. Accordingly, one must consider carefully how the Son could be sent into the world, who could not be absent from the world; or how he came into the world, from which he never withdraws: since certainly he to whom it is natural to fill the whole can in no way either withdraw or come. For that nature of immeasurable divinity is neither stretched out to fill what was empty before, nor drawn in to empty what it had filled before. And such is the power of the Creator, and such the condition of all creation, that just as no substance could exist unless he founded it, so no substance could endure unless he held it together. Accordingly, since according to the divinity God does not pass from place to place, the truth of the Christian faith holds that the Son of God is believed to have come into the world in this, that he is known to have received the form of a servant. For the Son of God came into the world when, with the equality of his Father's nature kept intact, he deigned to become a sharer in his mother's substance; when, his divinity kept intact, he became man; his eternity kept intact, temporal; his immensity kept intact, local; his unchangeableness kept intact, changeable; his immortality kept intact, mortal.

9. But the coming of the Son of God is not always understood in one and the same way. For he comes in one way when the Father sends [him], in another he deigns to come with the Father. For when he deigns to come with the Father, he comes as equal; but sent by the Father he came made a little lower than the angels. Sent by the Father, he is known to have come once; but with the Father he deigns to come innumerable times. For he set neither a manner nor a number of coming when he said: If anyone loves me he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him (John 14:23). Accordingly, that coming by which the Son alone came once from the Father into the world was shown not to the good alone but also to the wicked: to some that they might believe, to others that they might crucify; to some that they might be freed from sin, to others that they might have no excuse for their sin. For the Apostle shows that believers have been freed from sin, saying: But now, freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end, eternal life (Rom. 6:22). And the Saviour himself showed that unbelievers can have no excuse for their sin, saying: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now they have no excuse for their sin (John 15:22). For the Jews would not have had the sin of unbelief, had the Saviour's presence not also been shown to them. So that coming by which the Son was sent once by the Father into the world was for the fall and the rising of many; but that by which he comes with the Father pertains only to the rising of many, for charity merits it, which covers a multitude of sins. By that coming by which the Son was sent by the Father, he came once in the fullness of time; but by the one by which he is accustomed to come with the Father, from the beginning to the end of the world, to those to whom it was and is fitting, he neither ceased to come nor ceases. Hence it is that before he came in the flesh the prophets begged for his coming, saying: Stir up your might, and come to free us (Ps. 79:3). They would surely in no way have begged for the future coming of the Son of God if they did not have the grace of the same [Son] coming and dwelling in them.

10. This coming of the Son of God the Father those utterly repel from themselves who do not believe in the equality of the Father and the Son. For with the one who loves them, coming, they make one dwelling; but there cannot be one dwelling for them if the love is different. And if they are unequal, it is necessary that they be loved unequally. But for unequals one dwelling cannot be prepared in a single heart. Yet Scripture admonishes us, saying: Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart (Wis. 1:1). How then is God sought in simplicity of heart when a difference of love is shown to God the Father and God the Son? Or how is man's charity towards God simple if difference is thought to be in the divinity itself? Surely that divinity is loved with a simple heart which is believed to be simple by nature; but where a differing divinity is worshipped, not simplicity of heart but duplicity is shown: so the faith there is not true but feigned. But the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee what is feigned, and will remove himself from thoughts that are without understanding (Wis. 1:5). And the heart is proved double if ever someone thinks that not one divinity is to be worshipped by the faithful, or when he judges the nature of the Son not the same as the Father's. And if one who feigns goodness to his neighbour in words while bearing malice in his heart is called double-hearted, how is he who, under a pretence of truth, believes or says false things about God not held guilty of the crime of a double heart? For to divide what is by nature one in that supreme divinity, and to imagine a lesser and a greater God, most certainly belongs to the wickedness of a double heart. And holy Scripture says: Woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to evil-doing hands, and to the sinner who walks the earth by two ways (Ecclus. 2:14)! And since to think the divinity of Father and Son different is not to believe God (for he truly worships one God who worships no other at all, and he believes one God who does not believe there is another God), therefore the same Scripture continues, saying: Woe to those who do not believe God! for they are not protected by him (Ecclus. 2:15). Hence it is that our Saviour too, commending one divinity and lordship, says: No one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24). And we read that the Lord himself is God (Ps. 99:3). Hence it is certain that, with true faith and sincere charity, no one can serve [several] lords or gods. For there is one God of gods and Lord of lords, who is therefore alone to be worshipped, because he alone is by nature the true Lord God, who is the Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

11. Let us therefore, so that we may seek God in simplicity of heart, not believe even in [our] heart in a difference of divinity in the Father and the Son. But so that true simplicity of heart may remain in us, let that faith remain in us by which the one divinity of the Holy Trinity is believed and preached without difference. Thus the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, coming, deign to remain in us. The coming of the Holy Trinity to the one who loves it is one, by which the invisible God comes invisibly and invisibly makes [his] dwelling. And by remaining with the one who loves it, [the Trinity] itself multiplies the love on account of which it makes its dwelling in the man. For it comes for this reason, that it is loved; and by coming it brings about that it is loved more.

12. I have said these things so that you may know what kind of coming the Son's was when he was sent by the Father, and what kind the Son's coming is when he deigns to come with the Father. For just as in that coming, having been made man, he is recognised as less than the Father, so in this coming he is found to remain God equal to the Father. And the Holy Spirit too is said to come: since he too is, with the Father and the Son, one God, eternal and immeasurable by nature, without whom indeed neither the Father nor the Son can come. For he is known to love the Father and the Son who has charity in his heart. And the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). So the Father and the Son in no way come to the one who loves them without the Holy Spirit: for in order to come, they bestow, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, the charity by which they are loved. So the coming of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is always invisibly common [to them]: not by passing from place to place, but in this, that the Trinity itself, one God, deigns either to give the grace of charity so as to increase it, or to increase what it gives. But in another way the Son came, when the only-begotten God was made man for us: he who indeed, in the proper person of his divinity, received not the person of a man, but [his] nature. We know also that the Holy Spirit came visibly in the form of a dove: in a far different way indeed, that is, neither in that by which the Father and the Son come, not without the Holy Spirit, to the one who loves them, nor in this by which the Son alone came into the world, in that he wonderfully and uniquely received our nature in the person of his divinity. For the Holy Spirit did not receive the form of a dove as the Son received the form of a servant; nor was the Holy Spirit made in the likeness of doves as the Son was made in the likeness of the sons of men. So the Holy Spirit came in the form of a dove, not, certainly, taking a dove into unity of person. For the nature of doves did not need to be redeemed through the Holy Spirit as the nature of men was redeemed through the Son. For the Son took into the unity of his person that nature which he was without doubt going to redeem. And since his humanity is never separated from the Son of God, therefore he has lordship in heaven and on earth over all angels and all men. For according to human nature the Son of God humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8); and according to that nature God exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (ibid., 9). So when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4:4). And the Apostle, showing next why this was done, says: That he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. So human nature was taken up by the Son of God. And the only-begotten God was made man for this reason, that divine adoption might be given to us through him: that, since that man is true God by the natural truth of his divinity, we too, in that we are his brothers, might become sons of God, not by our merit but by his grace.

13. But the Holy Spirit, coming in the form of a dove, was not made a dove as the Son was made man; but through the form of a dove he showed that charity was to be given to us by his gift. For the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). And afterwards he appeared also in tongues of fire, but this too he did to signify the charity itself which he has bestowed on us. For since the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5); and in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through charity (Gal. 5:6); this is that simplicity of heart which was signified in the dove: for what we believe with the heart unto righteousness we must confess confidently with the mouth unto salvation. So the dove shows the simplicity of faith and charity, that we may believe rightly in God, and through God love our neighbour too. The fiery tongue also signifies the confession of true belief and the exhortation of holy charity. So that dove in whose form the Holy Spirit came upon Christ when he was baptised was made to signify something, and at once dissolved. For the Son alone took up human flesh and soul. For to him alone divine birth belonged by nature. And since he alone was born of the Father, he alone could also be born of the Virgin. Unless he had become man from man, he would not have been a sharer in our nature. So it came about that he received true flesh from the flesh of the Virgin, so that a true natural communion with him might remain for us. For how would he take either the ancient Fathers, or men of any time, into fellowship with his divinity, if he did not have a natural fellowship of flesh with them?

14. So the Son of God deigned to become not only man, but man from men. Hence it is that the Apostle says, speaking of Christ: For he did not take hold of angels, but took hold of the seed of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in all things, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted. Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him (Heb. 2:16–3:1). Hence it is that in another place of the same Epistle he says again: For every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. 5:1). And this high priest was such that, for the reconciliation of the human race, he offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet fragrance. Hence it is that when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). And so that the blessed Apostle might show that Christ the Son of God drew the origin of his flesh from that one man from whom natural unity has propagated all men, he therefore says in another place: For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. For which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will announce your name to my brothers (Heb. 2:11). And he says this of us who according to the flesh was both born and suffered for us: indeed, who became a sharer in our nature in such a way that he came from that one from whom we have all been made, and showed the origin of his flesh from that one from whom we all draw our origin. But if the Trinity took up flesh for us, since we have become brothers of him who was incarnate through fellowship of flesh, we would now be not only sons of God the Father but also brothers of the whole Trinity; and the one whom we have as Father in heaven, human birth would have made our brother as well.

15. It is [a mark] of great absurdity to suspect that he was begotten in time, whose property it is from eternity not to have been born, but to have begotten. So this befits the true faith: to confess that neither the Father nor the Spirit, but the Son, just as he alone was born of God the Father, so he alone was born of the Virgin Mary. Since, then, the Son alone, God, took up flesh, he therefore made us sons of God, and, freed from the slavery of sin, restored us to true freedom. And since he alone was born of the Virgin, he alone was therefore handed over for us: as the Apostle testifies, that God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all (Rom. 8:32). For he also says of the Son himself: And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me (Gal. 2:20). In another place too he says: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of God our Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages (Gal. 1:3–5). So just as the Father handed over the Son, so the Son handed himself over; and just as the Son gave himself, so the Father also gave him, as the Son says: For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life (John 3:16).

16. So, now that all these things are known, by which it is plainly shown that the Son alone took up flesh for our salvation, and that he alone was handed over for our sins and endured the punishment of suffering and death, far be it from any of the faithful to say that God the Father was either born of the Virgin or handed over for us. For these things belong to the Son alone, who, just as he deigned to be born in time for us, so deigned to die in time. But if anyone assigns the taking up of flesh to God the Father, let him pay particular attention to this in the Gospel: that God who put on flesh very often named himself not only son of man but also Son of God. For he himself said to the man born blind whom he had given sight: Do you believe in the Son of God? He answered and said: Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him? And Jesus said to him: You have both seen him, and he who is speaking with you is he. And he said: I believe, Lord. And falling down he worshipped him (John 9:35 ff.). To the Jews too he speaks thus: Is it not written in your law, I said, You are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, You blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God? (John 10:34–36). In another place too he called himself at once both Son of man and Son of God, saying: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life (John 3:14–15). There the Saviour at once added about himself what we have set down in this work, in which he named himself Son of God, saying: For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. He who believes in him will not be judged; but he who does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God (John 3:16 ff.). For also, when he named himself Son of man, saying to his disciples: Who do men say that the Son of man is? (Matt. 16:13), and, having heard the manifold opinion of men, namely of those who, about the Truth itself, were fashioning for themselves a deadly falsehood according to their own will, he had said: But who do you say that I am? — because Peter answered and said, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (ibid. 15–16), he therefore deserved to be called blessed, as the Lord himself replied: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed [this] to you, but my Father who is in heaven (ibid. 17).

17. Hence it is that even after the resurrection he testifies in these words that he will ascend to his Father: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17). If, then, God who put on flesh is asserted to be himself God the Father, it must follow that another is asserted to be the Father of the Father himself; and so God the Father too would have had a Father, to whom he could say: Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you (John 17:1). And from this sacrilegious sense, full of blasphemies, one falls back even into this: that there would now be thought to be not one Father but two; that is, one the Father of the Son, whom truth knows, and another the Father of the Father, whom vanity invents. And where then is it that the Apostle professes one God the Father, saying: But for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him (1 Cor. 8:6)? And in another place: One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all (Eph. 4:6). Though the Son is by nature one God with him, yet according to the persons, the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another. These persons blessed John shows plainly, saying: He who loves the begetter loves him who is born of him (1 John 5:1). Again he says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God (John 1:1–2); and shortly after, to show that flesh was taken up by the Word alone, he says: And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us (ibid. 14).

18. So God the Word became flesh, not the God with whom the Word was: for the only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, is full of grace insofar as he is flesh, and full of truth insofar as he is the Word: he himself, one, the Word made flesh who dwelt among us. Of him too the prophet says: This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who found out every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and lived among men (Bar. 3:36–38). True faith has received this testimony as spoken of the Son alone. For it is he who according to the flesh was seen on earth and lived among men. Hence the holy evangelist Matthew, fully in agreement with the prophetic word, says that Jesus lived among his disciples. For he says thus: And while they were living in Galilee, Jesus said to them: The Son of man is to be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again (Matt. 17:21–22). So he had come for this, to be killed for us. But how would he be killed if he were not handed over? Or how would he be handed over if he were not seized? And how would he be seized if he did not live among men, or how would he live among men if he were not seen on earth? And how would he be seen if he were not born? And how would he be born if he were not conceived as flesh from flesh? But if all these things did not happen, the counsel of the Lord, which abides for ever, would in no way be fulfilled. And if that counsel were void, no grace of salvation would be conferred on us sinners. And how would the name by which he was called Jesus be true in him? For this is interpreted Saviour. For this reason the angel, telling Joseph that Mary would bear the Son of God, also added this: And you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). And to Mary herself the angel spoke thus: Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High (Luke 1:31–32). So God the Father was not born of the Virgin, since he whom the Virgin bore was named Son of the Most High. Therefore, since there is one Father, and one Son, and one Holy Spirit, for this reason he who is by nature Son of the Most High from the eternal divinity of the Father is, according to the true faith, called the same Son of the Most High from the Virgin.

19. And do not be troubled that the prophet, speaking of the Son alone, said: This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him (Bar. 3:36). Nor let anyone, from his saying that no other is reckoned beside him, suppose that the Father is the same in person as the Son. Blessed Jeremiah, full of the Holy Spirit, says, This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, so that from his first saying, This is God, we might understand in this that no other is reckoned beside him, because there is no other God apart from him. For by nature there is likewise no other God apart from the Holy Spirit, because the Father is not one God, the Son another God, and the Holy Spirit another God; but the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, and apart from this our God there is no other God. Accordingly the Father is our God in such a way that no other is reckoned beside him; the Son too is our God in such a way that no other is reckoned beside him; no less is the Holy Spirit also our God in such a way that no other is reckoned beside him: because apart from this one God there is no other God, of whom David says: Who is God but the Lord, or who is God but our God? (Ps. 17:32). And God himself says: See, see that I am God, and there is no other besides me (Deut. 32:39). Of this blessed James too says: You believe that God is one; you do well; the demons also believe, and tremble (Jas. 2:19).

20. By nature, then, no other God is reckoned beside the Son, because no other God is reckoned beside the Father, nor is any other God reckoned beside the Holy Spirit. But in persons the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; nor is the Father himself the one who is the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the one who is the Father or the Son; but the same one God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit. And the Son himself shows that both the Father and the Holy Spirit are other in person, saying: There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the witness which he bears about me is true (John 5:32). And lest anyone think this was said of John, shortly after he says: But I have a witness greater than John. For the works which the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works which I do, bear witness about me, that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me (ibid. 36–37). He also shows that the Holy Spirit is personally another, saying: If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to abide with you for ever, the Spirit of truth (John 14:15–17); of whom he also says in another place: When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me (John 15:26). But the majesty of the Father and the Son is one, which did not descend from heaven to a place. For the supreme and true divinity cannot pass from place to place, because it is always whole everywhere. For the one majesty of the Trinity is the same as the one immeasurable divinity that is one by nature. But, as I said above, the nature of the Trinity is one in such a way that it is not one person. Accordingly the Son, while the immeasurableness of his majesty, which he has in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, remained, alone took human nature into the unity of his person. Therefore he does not share the flesh he took up with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit do not have a person in common.

21. So the whole Trinity made that form of a servant, which yet the Son alone took into his own person. For he alone is the Word, and the Evangelist truly says: The Word became flesh (John 1:14); yet the Father did not command him by some other word to become flesh: for the Father has one Word, through which he made and makes all things, through which he spoke and speaks all things. This Word was sent by the Father when the Word became flesh; but the Father did not speak to him with any passing words so that he should be sent. For the eternal Word born of the Father is the eternal command of the Father, because the eternal generation of the Son is itself the eternal speaking of the Father. This Word is heard by each person when the truth of the divinity and of the Incarnation is recognised. For just as each man has a word in his heart while he thinks, and that word is not brought outside unless it is clothed in a bodily voice, because through the voice it has taken on it can come to the knowledge of others; yet when that word is shown by the voice of the speaker, it is in no way separated from the inmost heart, but this happens wondrously, that it both reaches others whole by bodily speech and remains whole spiritually in the heart of the speaker; so too the Word of God the Father, born of the Father, remained in the Father: and it would in no way be recognised by us unless it were clothed with the substance of flesh as with a bodily voice. Thus the Word came whole to us when the Word became flesh, and remained whole and spiritual with the Father: equal to the Father, of whom it is ever born, and, so that it could be grasped by us, made less on account of the flesh it took. And so the Lord from the Lord remained Lord in the form of God, and, to come to the servants, took from a handmaid the reality of the form of a servant.

22. But some who understand too little the mystery of this form of a servant taken up, when they hear us preach that the essence of the holy Trinity is one, either deny or doubt that it could have happened that the Son, whom we preach to be inseparable from the Father and the Holy Spirit according to the divinity, should both alone take for us the reality of the form of a servant and nonetheless remain inseparable from the Father and the Holy Spirit. But this would doubtless seem impossible to those who do not perceive the invisible things of God through the things that have been made, because they do not understand them. If they paid attention to the common condition of human nature, they would find the right lines of understanding even in that great sacrament of godliness. Since, then, there is one true divinity which has in itself three wholly inseparable persons, for which reason the Trinity itself is one God, and in creatures no nature is found inseparable in three persons, let us consider what takes place in each man, in whom we find not three persons in one nature, but two natures in one person. For God, by a wondrous work of power, composed the one nature of man out of two natures, that is, a rational soul and flesh, and ordained that the one person of man should abide in soul and flesh. See, in man there are two natures in one person: so we say that the Trinity is three persons in one nature.

23. Let us note, then, that here certain things are done in common by these two natures abiding in one person, which are not received or possessed in common. Indeed we find in ourselves that something is done by the one joint office of flesh and soul which we nevertheless assign either to the flesh alone or to the soul. For most certainly, just as the flesh alone is fed by bodily foods, so the soul is nourished spiritually by the word of God. And yet, for the flesh, which was made from earth, to be fed with earthly foods, it eats with the soul working together, since it lives from the soul, and it eats because it lives, usefully having within itself the office of the other, the soul, working together with it, so that it has at once from life the power to eat, and from food the means to live. So when food is taken, the operation is common to flesh and soul; yet that food is found to belong properly to the flesh alone. Also in receiving the word of God, the spiritual food by which the soul alone is fed, it uses the office of the eyes or the ears to reach that food. And so its being fed inwardly is not accomplished without the working of the flesh. Just as here, then, the operation of both natures is found, though the receiving belongs to one, so let us believe that the human nature of the only-begotten of God was made by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together, but taken up by the Son alone, in mercy, for our salvation.

24. You add, meanwhile, that one of you said afterwards at that banquet that God did not make flies, fleas, scorpions and bugs, but that after the casting down of that unworthy angel, the devil, all these were made by the devil himself. And when you said that God made all things, and these very good, he said that you ought to consult me about this, so that I might satisfy them on this: whether these were made before the transgression, when God made all things, or after the transgression. These are the words with which your letter ends. This question has two parts. For you have asked both whether God made all those things, and when he made them.

25. First, then, I see that I must discuss whether God made them. Here blessed John the Evangelist shows us what we ought to think, saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3). See how the holy Evangelist, filled with the Spirit of God, in a few words has made known to us for our salvation not only the Creator but also the creature. For what he says, In the beginning was the Word, the right faith understands in two ways: that is, either that the Son was in the Father, because by nature the Father and the Son are one beginning; or that not only the Father but also the Son is without beginning. For that is most certainly called the true beginning which is preceded by no beginning of existence; but whatever began to be in a beginning was made by the work of God creating, and cannot have one nature with the Creator: for what God created out of nothing is subject to a beginning. Accordingly that is rightly said to be in the beginning to which it is natural always to be without a beginning of existence: and this eternity without beginning is itself the true divinity. This is found by nature in the one Son, who is born of the Father, and in the one Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. So what the Evangelist says, In the beginning was the Word, is as if he said: The Word always was. For whatever beginning a man can conceive, that Word is not found at any time to have begun, but always to be in the beginning. Then, saying, the Word was with God, he shows that the nature of the Word is neither temporal nor local. For the Word which was in the beginning has nothing of a beginning in time; it has nothing of extent in place, since it was with God before every creature subject to times or places. Then saying, the Word was God, he shows the one nature of the Father and the Son, since he said that the Word which was with God was by nature nothing other than God. For the Evangelist, saying Word first, expressed the name of a truly existing person, which is certainly not common to the Father and the Son. For the Son alone is called the Word.

26. The meaning of nature required, moreover, that just as the name of the person, so also the name of the nature should be shown in the Word. Therefore the blessed Evangelist went on to add: And the Word was God, and so he fulfilled the office of holy preaching by indicating the only-begotten Son of God not only as a person but also as a nature: by calling him Word, a personal name, he showed the Son of the Father, and by naming him God, a common name, he showed that he is of one nature with the Father. Then, so that the unity of nature might be commended more strongly by the unity of the work, the blessed Evangelist added: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Who said this? Surely the one who, reclining on the breast of Wisdom and Truth, received true knowledge of the incomprehensible eternity; who, just as he knew that the Father and the Son are one God, so also knew that all things were made by the Father through the Son. Hence holy John took in all the things that were made through the Son so universally as to say: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. So whoever strives to deny that flies, fleas, scorpions and bugs, or any other things by which mortal sense is offended, were made by God, must either say that they were not made at all, or, if he says they were made, [say that they were] not made by the Father through the Son. What else remains, then, but that he should say that the evangelist John lied in his preaching? For he says: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

27. So there is nothing which the Father, who made all things, did not make; nor is there anything which the Father did not make through the Son, without whom nothing was made. Therefore whatever is by nature something must be counted among the works of him through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. The Evangelist, full of truth, bears witness [to this], and no less Paul too, the vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, did not cease to make it known to us in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, saying what we have already set down above: But for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him (1 Cor. 8:6). He took care to set out these same things more plainly in another place, saying: For in him all things were founded in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions, or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all, and all things hold together in him (Col. 1:16, 17). But lest anyone, hearing that all things in heaven and on earth were created through Christ and in Christ, should suppose, because the sea is not named here, that the things which are in the waters are foreign to the work of divine creation, let him first attend to the beginning of Genesis itself, where at the Lord's command the waters brought forth creeping things with souls, and birds that fly above the earth (Gen. 1:20); and let him recognise that he who is the creator of trees and plants on earth, and likewise of the lights and stars in heaven, is himself the creator of fishes and birds in the waters. And just as he knows that God first made the heaven in which he would make the lights and stars, and first made the earth which at his bidding would bring forth plants and trees, so [let him know that God] made the waters, from which at his word creeping and flying things alike came forth. For he would not have created anything from the waters by the Word, if he had not first made those same waters by the Word. Hence blessed David did not keep silent that heaven, earth and sea, with all that is in them, were made by God, universally, saying: Blessed is the man whose helper is the God of Jacob, his hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them (Ps. 145:4, 5). Since, then, prophetic authority testifies that heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, were made by God, and Paul the apostle also asserts that all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions, or Principalities or Powers, were created in Christ, by what reasoning or by what truth does anyone refuse to believe that flies and scorpions, fleas and bugs on earth were created by him by whom he cannot deny that Thrones, Dominions, Principalities and Powers in the heavenly places were created? Is that God, then, who by creating established the angelic legions above the heaven, to be denied to make scorpions on the earth, on which he made men, made beasts and cattle, made birds and fishes?

28. What, I ask, is displeasing in these scorpions, that anyone should think they were not made by God? For there is nothing in the body of a scorpion which does not point to the praise of the Creator. First, the very structure of the limbs, joined together and proportioned, the fit and balance of the parts; then the soul that gives life and sense to the body: who would doubt that all these are good? But surely [what is objected is] that force of venom which is found harmful to men, and so is thought dreadful in the body of the scorpion. Would that men learned here to consider the punishment of their own transgression, and ceased falsely to assign the good works of God to the devil! For they pay too little attention to how much natural fittingness counts among the works of God, how much due measure benefits each single thing, and how much the excess of immoderation harms. [...] since almighty God did not allow it to be great, who would not praise the works of God even in these very scourges, when he sees a sinner chastised by a divine blow? For God made man upright, as it is written (Eccles. 7:30), and established him as lord of all the things which he had created on land and sea in such a way as to make him subject to his own power alone, requiring from him the due obedience of service, while he had given him free choice of will. As long as he served his Lord with fitting devotion, he also held a power of unshaken dominion over those things above which he himself stood; nor did he lose anything of what he had received, so long as he himself rendered in full what he owed. But offending the Lord by transgressing the command, the despiser at once found in his own body the insult that he had shown to God, so that he might learn how evil it was to despise the precepts of the good Creator, when he himself, after he had begun to be evil, had lost his power over his genital members. How, then, could he remain lord of all those things which he had received from God, who, despising the Lord, had lost the rights of dominion in his own body first? From then on that very body too began to be subject to infirmities and to death; and so, by just ensuing punishment, it came about that he who did not fear the death of the soul in sin should fear the death of the body in punishment, and that, having lost the rest which he enjoyed when blessed, he should, most wretched, be troubled by the tiniest animals.

29. Hence it is that, after the sin of the first man, by which human nature was universally made subject to the reign of sin and death, man is master of camels, horses, oxen, elephants and the other great four-footed beasts, yet is shaken by the bite of a bug or a flea; and while all those which are larger in body and stronger in might serve man tamely, these tiniest things, which can very easily be crushed and killed with just two fingers, can in no way be brought, that is, recalled, to tameness. It is clear that this was done by divine judgement so that from those over which man is master he might learn how great a dignity he had before the transgression, and from those by which he is troubled and hurt he might recognise to how great a downfall he came by the transgression. God left the greater things in his power and withdrew the lesser, showing at once what the Creator's goodness conferred on man and what the sinner's own wickedness brought upon him. So through the transgression of the first humans, in requital for so great a crime, a severe natural infirmity befell the human race, not so that man would yield to certain evil natures, but so that human infirmity would feel punishments and dangers from the unfittingness of good natures [to one another]. That a flea torments a man, then, and a scorpion kills him, is not a creation of evils but an unfittingness of good natures, which followed from the equity of the judge when the wickedness of contumacious man came first. For holy Zacharias in his prayer most rightly confesses that God, whose works are true and whose ways are right, being supremely good, [makes] all things whatsoever he makes [...]

30. Hence it is that by a wonderful working he uses fittingly even that very unfittingness of natures by which human sins are punished, since unchangeable justice, which gives to each its own, so acts as to make the unfittingness of each nature to another fit universally with its own works. Any nature, however, when it is less fitted to another nature for [that one's] health, is not to be thought evil on the ground that it harms (for every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good); rather, it is often for this reason that harm is inflicted on one nature by some other nature, because infirmity yields and succumbs to unfittingness. For often the very things, that is, the very natures, in which alone undoubted destruction is usually found, if they are tempered by a more moderate fit with other things, are turned from a danger of death into remedies for health; and this we find first in the venomous animals themselves. For some say that whenever 'sacred fire' arises in the body, it is quickly extinguished by applying crushed scorpions. But even if this is perhaps thought by some either doubtful or false, no one is allowed to deny what is wonderfully found in serpents. No one is unaware that vipers are by nature venomous, since they kill scorpions with their venomous sting; and yet, to show that it is not the evil but the unfittingness of natures that harms, we know that from the flesh of vipers, tempered by the fit of other things, medicines are made against the bites of vipers, and are applied with healing effect not only to those who are stung by scorpions but also to those who are bitten by vipers. Who would not marvel at the wisdom of God here? Who would not magnify his goodness and praise his foresight? For, not withholding his mercies in his anger, from the very source from which he caused dangers to arise for sinners he established that help should be supplied to those in danger, so that we who feel discomforts because of our wickedness might feel benefits from his goodness. Who could set out the praise of the Creator in adequate words, when he so created one and the same viper that it bears in itself both destruction and remedy at once; and that what brings death while living restores health when dead; and that it both brings on and drives off the ruin of life; and that the venom poured in by the serpent's tooth is extinguished by the flesh of the same serpent? So it comes about that the viper which while living served human infirmity and death, when dead serves life and health. Who, I ask, does these things but he of whom the Church sings mercy and judgement (Ps. 100:1)?

31. The substance called scammony: who does not know how much it harms the healthy if it is taken on its own, and how much it benefits the sick if it is fittingly mixed with other substances? And to speak of things that are always sought by everyone, and whose daily use is found to be needed not only by infirmity but also by the very health of human life, let us consider bread and wine, neither of which suits someone with a fever. For we see that doctors always forbid drink to the sick, and sometimes even the food of bread. This is done not because bread or wine are evil, but because they do not suit the sick person. For afterwards, when they have begun to suit him, they both nourish strength and preserve health; yet taking them without measure takes vigour away from the strong, while it forces the healthy man to fall ill. See how much due measure and the fittingness of things count for in God's creatures, to which lack of measure and unfittingness are found to be opposed. When [harm] in them is called natural, what is found is not a natural evil but an accidental infirmity; and this anyone easily finds in all creatures who so considers the good things created by the supreme good that he recognises in them the inexpressible and indescribable praise of the Creator; and through this, he himself is to be loved above all, who even in those things which we feel as penal because of our wickedness is found both merciful and just, since he relieves the frail from the very source by which he restrains the contumacious; and because, when pride came first, misery at once followed in man, the Lord, merciful and just, applies the relief of mercy from the very source from which he imposes the weight of pride.

32. Nevertheless, whoever that son of the Church is who, as you say, put forward those [claims], asserting that flies, scorpions, fleas and bugs were made not by God but by the devil, let him take care not to be misled and deceived by the deadly cunning of the Manichaeans, who, themselves set in darkness, strive to introduce a god of light and a god of darkness, and to preach two principles naturally opposed to each other. Hence, because they call the nature of light good and the nature of darkness evil, they are led by their own error to the point that they do not hesitate to assert that among all things in the world some natures are good and some evil: calling those evil by which their senses are offended, and those good by whose delight they are soothed, understanding neither, as the Apostle says, what they say nor the things about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7). For, to say something about light and darkness, whose natures they think chiefly opposed, is not their assertion found false first of all in this, that darkness, which they say is naturally opposed to light, is found to have no nature at all? For light and darkness are not two natures; but where there is no light, the very absence of light is called by the name of darkness; just as the absence of sound is called silence, just as the absence of clothing is called nakedness, just as a vessel is called empty into which no substance, whether of liquid or of anything else, is poured: so in ourselves it is called hunger where there is no food, and it is called thirst where there is no drink.

33. All these things, then, that I have mentioned, and others like them which I have now passed over in silence to keep the discussion within measure, are indeed without doubt opposites, yet not through their own natures, but through possession and privation, that is, through that opposition by which something is either had or not had. Accordingly, although they are opposites, their effects are not always found to be opposite. For this bodily light, which the Manichaeans consider the principal good, although it is indeed good, since it was created by the supreme good, is yet good only to such a degree that the substance of life is by nature to be preferred to it; so although it is good, yet for those who use it unfittingly it sometimes becomes not healthful but penal: it invigorates healthy eyes, tortures sick ones; it refreshes the sound, dulls those in pain. On the contrary, eyes in pain obtain some rest from darkness, and with doors and windows closed they feel some relief from the pain they suffer from the light, and are nourished for seeing the light by a certain fittingness of darkness. See: the less light suits, the more it hurts; and the more darkness suits, the more it helps; and just as the brightness of light helps healthy eyes, so the obscurity of darkness is accustomed to help those in pain; and so, when each is received fittingly, an effect of both light and darkness is found in helping the eyes. For just as the healthy are helped by light, so the sick are refreshed by darkness. For when tired eyes are closed in sleep, they are in a way helped by darkness so that they are made sound and strong again for seeing the light. It is the same for sick and tired eyes to be withdrawn from good light to restore health and strength as it is for the whole body, when it falls ill, to be held back from its customary taking of food: foods are not contrary and harmful to the sick because they are naturally evil, but because they do not suit their infirmity; for infirmity does not bear all that health takes in. Hence sometimes by the same things that refresh a healthy body, the infirmity of the body is weighed down; so that sometimes even the healthy body itself is harmed by excess of the things by whose use it is helped, and when something is taken unfittingly, where health is sought to be preserved, infirmity is found. The very use of clothing too, if it is unfitting, is found to be not healthful but harmful. For who, whether through some poverty or through bodily infirmity, would not harm himself by using winter garments when he is hot, or summer ones when he is cold?

34. It would take long to show by many examples the judgement of fittingness, since they cannot be lacking to those who look. Accordingly, all natures that exist, that live, that feel, that understand, since they were made by God, that is, by the supreme good, are good: if they were not made by the supreme good, they would not be good; and if they were not good, they would have nothing of good in themselves. And first, since life is one of the goods, and such a good as is loved by living men, if there were any nature not made by the supreme good, it would in no way live. This I say of animals, that is, of substance that lives and feels; but those natures too that neither live nor feel have the very fact that they exist from the creation of him who supremely is: because not only to live but also to be is good, and what supremely is, is the supreme good.

35. So there is no evil nature, whether living or not living; and through this all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good. But some of them, though good by God's creation, have become penal to man through the punishment of sin, not because of their own nature but because of man's fault. In this it has been shown to man, made in the image of God, how great an evil he brought on himself, who has been brought to this point, that the ruin of death is inflicted on him by tiny little beasts. Therefore in all animals, in all plants, and in all creatures universally, whatever man sees to be deadly to himself, let him not say that an evil nature is in them, but let him recognise in them the punishment of his own wickedness. For we became like fleas and bugs after we became contumacious towards God; and the scorpion's sting became deadly to man after he of his own will preferred to be wounded by the sting of death. For the sting of death is sin (1 Cor. 15:56): with this sting man first so struck himself to death that he made it pass through his offspring too; so that even those in whom the grace of God makes sin not reign do not lack frequent and manifold danger from the punishment of sin. For this is why even just men, living holy lives, are not free in this mortal life from troubles and dangers of this kind: because as long as they live mortally, they are not without sin. Hence blessed John says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8). The holy apostle James too testifies that in many things we all offend (James 3:2).

36. But the sins of the saints are not such as are the sins of the wicked. For the sins of the saints are light, the sins of the wicked grave. In the sins of the wicked, either human perversity thinks wrongly about God, or human desire leads man to (other reading: through) the desires of the flesh, or human cruelty harms his neighbour. For of those who sin against God, Wisdom says: But those who sin against me act impiously against their own souls; and those who hate me love death (Prov. 8:36). Of those who live luxuriously the Apostle says: But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are. Let no one deceive you (1 Cor. 3:17-18). Speaking also of hatred of a brother, blessed John says: He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now. For he who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him. But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is walking, because the darkness has blinded his eyes (1 John 2:9-11).

37. The sins of the wicked, then, come about in three (other reading: all) ways. For they are entangled either in sacrileges, or in shameful deeds, or in crimes. They commit sacrileges when they do not think rightly about God, and depart from the true faith either through fear for temporal advantages, or through mere blindness and perversity of heart. They sin in shameful deeds when, immoderate and obscene in themselves, they live basely. They sin in crimes when they cruelly harm others either with losses or with any oppressions whatever. Both kinds, however, whether sinning mortally in faith or in works, the blessed Apostle calls reprobate, saying of those who contradict the true faith: But just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these too resist the truth, men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith (2 Tim. 3:8). Likewise rebuking those who, under profession of the true faith, live in evil works and crimes, he says: To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; but both their mind and conscience are polluted. They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds, since they are abominable, and unbelieving, and reprobate for every good work (Titus 1:15-16). But when the saints sin, they so succumb in any sin to human weakness or human delight (other reading: love) that they neither obstinately contradict the true faith, nor pollute themselves with shameful deeds, nor harm their neighbours with crimes: which the blessed Apostle shows, saying: For the grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, and justly, and piously in this world (Titus 2:11-12). The same blessed apostle indeed admonishes us in another place, saying: Not to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety (Rom. 12:3). Nevertheless, in this threefold division in which he says that we should live soberly, and justly, and piously in this world, it seems to me that he lives soberly who does not follow the delights of luxury; he lives justly who in no way harms his neighbour, and bestows benefits on him as far as he is able; he lives piously who on no account departs from the fellowship of ecclesiastical unity, and, placed within the Church, holds without doubting those things which he knows most certainly to belong to the knowledge of the true faith; but those things of which he is ignorant or about which he doubts, he humbly and patiently searches out, until, if he thinks otherwise in anything, he comes to know it by God's revealing it to him.

38. This sobriety, justice, and piety (other reading: and peace), which ought to be present in all the faithful, are so joined to one another that if one of them is lacking, the other which seems to be present profits nothing at all. For the sobriety by which someone abstains in himself from shameful deeds does not save (other reading: is not sound) unless it is pious and just, that is, unless he both believes rightly in God and gladly bestows on his neighbour what charity demands; nor is that justice fruitful by which each one bestows on his neighbour what he delights to have bestowed on himself, if it is not sober and pious; piety too, by which one believes rightly in God, is dead if either sobriety of conduct or charity towards the neighbour is not maintained. True salvation of the soul is therefore acquired when piety in faith, and justice in charity, and sobriety in chastity and frugality are maintained.

39. We are taught by the divine utterances that the saints sin in one way and the wicked in another. For Hagar, Sarah's maidservant, would not have been driven out had she not been proud (Gen. 21); and Sarah herself would not have been blamed had she not laughed (Gen. 18). For the one became proud, seeing that she had conceived; the other laughed, doubting that she would conceive. Both are found to have sinned, but the sin of each is not found to be equal: for in one of them human weakness doubted; but in the other human rashness contumaciously exalted itself. Therefore Hagar deserved to be driven out by a command of divine severity, while Sarah deserved to be blamed with the gentle mildness of the divine voice. And because the sin in that doubt was light, strengthened by the word of the divine promise she cast off doubt and received most certain faith, through which she also received the power to conceive: which apostolic authority attests, saying: By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of seed, even beyond the time of life, because she believed him faithful who had promised (Heb. 11:11).

40. We find in another place that the sins of the saints and of the wicked are not equal; but the former are light, needing to be purged by temporal correction, while the latter are grave, deserving to be punished by the perpetual burning of eternal fire. For at the water of contradiction the children of Israel sinned in one way (Num. 20:13), being rebellious against God in every way; Moses in another, who did not contradict God out of rashness, but through weakness presumed too little on God's working; made like blessed Peter, who heard from the Lord: O you of little faith, why did you doubt? (Matt. 14:31). Hence the contumacy of the Israelites deserved to be condemned with eternal punishment; but in Moses the punishment of that sin went only so far that entry into the land of promise alone was denied him. For Moses himself too testified that the Lord was angry with him not on account of his own sin but on account of them, saying in Deuteronomy: Nor is the indignation against the people any wonder, since the Lord, angry with me also on your account, said: Nor shall you enter there (Deut. 1:37). And holy David too shows that Moses was afflicted on account of that very sin of the people, saying: And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted on account of them (Ps. 105:32). So the people provoked the Lord, Moses doubted the Lord's work; and because the sin of that provocation and of that doubt was not equal, therefore holy Moses, although he was afflicted for them, was nevertheless not condemned with them to eternal punishment.

41. And so that we may briefly look at something in the very practice of human life, from which we may more easily take an example, let us take the souls of baptised people as being like women joined in marriage. For the Apostle commends the great sacrament of marriage itself in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5:32). Any soul, then, that clings faithfully to Christ is like a wife living faithfully with her husband: who, within the very chastity of marriage, often saddens her husband's mind, yet keeps faith with the marriage bed in pure chastity, and manages her husband's property prudently and temperately; and so she both sins against her husband and yet lives chastely and faithfully with her husband; and she whom human weakness sometimes makes offend against her husband, conjugal chastity makes cling sweetly to her husband. But that woman who, whether she has gone out of her husband's house or remains in the same dwelling of her husband, has been mingled in adultery and has squandered her husband's property, is judged not worthy of pardon, but is held liable to deadly guilt. Such is the soul which, consenting to the devil, is either overthrown by unbelief or entangled in crimes.

42. Of such the Apostle says that neither fornicators, nor servers of idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:9-10). But of those who sin lightly it is said: Seven times the just man falls, and rises again (Prov. 24:16). Such a man is both said to sin and yet is truly called just. For he does not so fall as to cease to be just, since it is written: When the just man falls, he will not be thrown into confusion, because the Lord strengthens his hand (Ps. 36:24). The Lord, then, is present even to the just man as he falls, because he does not so sin that the Lord departs from him. For he has concupiscence from the weakness of the flesh, but does not consent to concupiscence, strengthened by the power of spiritual grace.
