This concupiscence is the law of sin, placed even in the members of the saints; from which, however, the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord frees his just ones: who for this reason bore our sins in his body upon the tree, that, separated from our sins, we might live with justice (1 Pet. 2:24). When, therefore, the just man falls, he contracts debts; but the debts of the just man are such as can be forgiven in daily prayer, when he truthfully says: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt. 6:12).

43. The sins of the just, then, come from the necessity of weakness; the sins of the wicked come from the intention of a most evil will. In the former the beginning of sin is found in such a way that its effect does not follow. For although it arises through weakness, it is overcome through the grace of God. But the latter, deprived of the help of grace (other reading: fittingly), an evil will hurls headlong wherever depraved desire has led. Therefore the faults of the saints are said to be sins, not crimes: for which they are so corrected by the father that they are not condemned by the judge: yet this correction belongs to judgement, but a fatherly one, by which God mercifully both judges and scourges his sons, in order to rescue them from the punishment of everlasting damnation. Showing this, the blessed Apostle says: If we judged ourselves, we would surely not be judged; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world (1 Cor. 11:31-32). Blessed Peter also affirms this, saying: For it is the time for judgement to begin from the house of God. If, then, it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the just man will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear (other reading: will appear [sing.])? (1 Pet. 4:17-18).

44. Let no faithful and wise person, then, call the faith of the saints weak, if ever he sees that the trouble of some adversity has befallen them in the time of this life. For bodily health and sickness befall the faithful and the unfaithful, the good and the bad, in common; and therefore the adversity of bodily sickness touches both in common, because sometimes health too is given temporally to both in common. For the just are distinguished from the wicked not by bodily condition, but by faith and life. They endure together, in the body, the troubles and dangers of the present life, which they nevertheless bear with an entirely different intention. And they do not groan equally in the evils of this life because they do not love the goods of this life equally. For the wicked want to have the present life tranquil, without troubles, so that they may not lack goods that are perishable and temporal; but the just hate the dangers and troubles of the present life so that they may fully enjoy God, whom they love: seeking true rest in him in whom they are to have everlasting blessedness. Accordingly, they do not love temporal goods, which they know will soon cease; and for this reason in their use they do not seek what may satisfy desire, but what may refresh charity and sustain weakness; nor do they seek from them joy as from a domestic delight, but, as from provision for a journey, a modest comfort suited to the needs of things (other reading: of the guilty).

45. And since we are now disputing the opinion of a man who does not believe that flies and scorpions, fleas and bugs, could have been made by God, we must also guard against this: that he may have conceived this view, wholly foreign to the catholic faith, not from the error of the Manichaeans but from reading the divine Scriptures. For the law is good, if one uses it lawfully (1 Tim. 1:8). And he does not use the law lawfully who does not understand from the words of the law what he ought to understand. I have said this because we read in Exodus (7:10) that the rod of Moses which Aaron carried was turned into a serpent by divine operation; where it is also said (ibid., 12) that the magicians of Pharaoh, whom the Apostle calls Jannes and Jambres, did likewise, so that their rods were turned into serpents by magical incantations (2 Tim. 3:8). Then, when Aaron struck the waters of the river and they were turned into blood (Exod. 7:20), sacred Scripture records that the same was done likewise by their incantations (ibid., 22). Afterwards also, when Aaron struck the waters and brought forth frogs, which at once covered the land of Egypt, those sorcerers too, striving against him with their unspeakable arts, are related to have done similar things (Exod. 8:6-7). But after it came to the point that gnats were to be brought forth from the struck earth (ibid., 17-18), the wickedness of the magic art could work nothing of the kind. Here, first, this man who asserts that flies were made by the devil should recognise that he is a liar, since the devil and his angels, even though they were permitted to do other things, nevertheless failed in the work of the flies. Here who does not see that those transgressors made serpents from rods, or brought forth frogs from the waters, because God permitted it; but could not make gnats, that is, flies, because God did not permit it?

46. Sometimes, however, by the hidden and incomprehensible judgement of God, evil angels are permitted to do certain things, in order to test the good and to lead astray the wicked; yet they do not themselves create what they do, but are permitted to bring forth, from the hidden bosom of God the Creator, which we cannot see, something that we can see. Thus the devil could be the creator neither of serpents nor of frogs, although he brought them forth with God's permission; just as he was not the creator of fire when, to test Job, he consumed his sheep together with the shepherds by fire falling from heaven (Job 1:16); just as he was not the creator of the wind when a great wind, rushing from the desert, struck the four corners of the house and crushed all the sons of holy Job together in one collapse. Diverse natures, then, that is, the elements of this world, God almighty alone created; and in their secret and hidden depths he placed certain seeds of things, hidden from us but manifest to the angels: of which, as the fitness of the work and of the time requires, by the hidden counsel of his wisdom, God either commands certain things to be brought forth through good angels or permits them to be displayed through evil ones. And by permitting these things God shows how great a power he has caused to be in the holy angels, when he grants even to the evil ones the ability to do certain marvels out of bodily creation itself. Hence it is that our Saviour too does not cease to forewarn his faithful, saying: For false christs and false prophets will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that (if it can be) even the elect will be led into error (Mark 13:22). For the blessed Apostle too, speaking of the Antichrist, says: That wicked one will be revealed, whom our Lord Jesus Christ will kill with the breath of his mouth, and will destroy by the brightness of his coming: whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power, and lying signs and wonders, and in all the seduction of iniquity, for those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them the working of error, so that they believe a lie, and that all may be judged who have not believed (other reading: do not believe) the truth, but have consented to iniquity (2 Thess. 2:8 ff.).

47. By these and similar testimonies we shall know that all natures were created by divine work, and that whatever harms us ought not to be called evil by nature, but is found unfitting for us because of our weakness. From this, however, a fitting warning is given to us, that with a humble heart we should fear the justice of divine power. But that not only evil angels, but not even good angels, are creators of natures, no wise man either believes or says. For God, as we said above, made all things in wisdom, and this wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). And it orders all things because in it the Father made all things. Just as, therefore, God created angels in the heavens in wisdom, so in the same wisdom he created little worms on earth; and he who established Thrones, Dominions, Principalities and Powers on high, he himself made scorpions, fleas and bugs on earth. He who created the hen, he himself created the fly: but he gave the latter by which proud man may be confounded, the former by which the weak may be refreshed. Hence it is that from the one he willingly receives food, from the other he unwillingly suffers nausea: so that, at least, he is compelled not only to see God's comfort in the one, but also to see in the other the desert of his own sin.

48. Accordingly, let this man take care not to be led astray by that name by which the prince of demons is called Beelzebub in the Gospel, which is interpreted 'prince of flies'. For this was not said because the devil could create flies: for the angel too, speaking to the prophet Daniel, says: And behold, Michael, one of the first princes, came to my help (Dan. 10:13); and a little later: There is no one who helps me in all these things except Michael your prince (ibid., 21). And we find not only angels but also men called princes. For it is written: The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham (Ps. 46:10); and it is said to the Church: In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will establish them as princes over all the earth (Ps. 44:17). And in the book of Moses (Gen. 25:16) we know that princes of tribes are named. Yet because men or angels are called princes, they are not on that account to be called creators not only of angels or men, but also of any irrational souls whatever, or of any bodies whatever. For Beelzebub himself, whose name is interpreted 'prince of flies', is certainly called prince of demons: over whom, however, he holds princely rule as the first author and instigator of wickedness, not as creator and founder of nature. For the evil angels have God as the maker of their nature; but they have the devil as the prince of their wickedness. For the whole multitude of the runaway angels was made good by God, by whose gratuitous kindness it came about that they existed; but by their own will they clung to the devil, so as to fall. Accordingly he is called their prince, not because he created them, but because he dragged them with him into the precipice of perdition. In that, therefore, the devil is called prince of flies, he is shown to be prince of the wicked, whom another Scripture signifies, saying: Dying flies destroy the oil of sweetness (Eccles. 10:1). Who destroy [it], except those who grieve the Holy Spirit either by the crime of unbelief or by the sordid obscenity (other reading: obscurity) of unclean works, while they defile themselves either by perverse belief or by depraved conduct? Forbidding this with concern, the Apostle says: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed for the day of redemption (Eph. 4:30).

49. They destroy, then, the oil of sweetness in themselves who do not use the sacrament of spiritual grace with a right order of life. But though they thus destroy it, the oil itself cannot be destroyed, just as, though they grieve [him] according to their evil will, the Holy Spirit cannot feel any sorrow. For of the Son of God himself it is said to the Hebrews: How much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled on the Son of God (Heb. 10:29)! But the Son of God is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, which is in no way trampled on, because it is in no way defiled. For of it it is said in the book (other reading: books) of Wisdom: For it reaches everywhere because of its purity; and therefore nothing defiled runs into it. For it is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness (Wis. 7:24 ff.). The wicked, then, grieve the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit cannot be grieved; the wicked trample on the Son of God, but the Son of God is in no way trampled on.

50. Now the saying that the wicked grieve the Holy Spirit and trample on the Son of God, while both the Son of God and the Holy Spirit (other reading: [Spirit] of God) remain incapable of being grieved or trampled on, is like what the Saviour says in the Gospel: Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5:28). But if, while he commits adultery, she remains chaste, how much more, while the wicked grieve and trample, does the divine substance of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit remain without sorrow and blessed!

51. Let none of the faithful, then, say that any nature could have been created in its origin by the devil, lest, while he affirms that any animals came into being by the devil's creating, he should consequently ascribe to the works of the devil also those things from which they take their origin. For certain kinds of flies arise either from the refuse of bodies or from rotted plants or flesh. Often we see some flies born even from pulses. And the weevil, too, commonly comes into being from grain. Whoever, then, asserts that animals of this kind were created not by God but by the devil, why should he not also assert that the wood, grain, pulses, plants and flesh from which they are born were made [by him]? And so, consequently, when he sees worms taking their origin not only from human corpses but even from living bodies, since in worms of human mortality a fleshly sense is sometimes shown, he will without doubt proclaim the devil the author of human bodies too. But since one who believes rightly and understands rightly would not dare to assign the origin of any creature even to the good angels themselves, how does this man assign the power or authority to create any animal to an angel cast down and shut out from his dignity by the vice of his own depravity? No one would dare to assign this to him even if he had remained in angelic dignity and goodness without any vice.

52. It is not for nothing that at the very beginning of Genesis, the Scripture, speaking of all things that were made, affirms that God made all things, saying of each one: And God made, and God saw that it was good (Gen. 1). All these he completed on the sixth day, and among them nothing could be lacking that would be made afterwards. For God, foreknowing what was to come, just as he knew that man would sin, so out of all the things he made he prepared for him, for his health, not only comforts but also scourges. For one and the same is the hand of a good father, which gives his son both food and the scourge: the one that he may live, the other that he may live well; the one that he may not fail from weakness, the other that he may not, undisciplined, despise his father's commands: For whom the Lord loves he chastens, and he scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6). Nor does it profit anything to abound in temporal goods, if by living badly one lacks the everlasting ones; and when he has lacked these, he must be consigned to perpetual evils, which he cannot be without.

53. Let each one, therefore, restrain the rashness of his thinking; and just as with the things in which he delights, so also with the things by which he is offended, let him not doubt that they were made by God in their nature. His wisdom, reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly, shows the beauty of its work even in those things which corruption destroys; showing also in the tiniest animals the grace of each one's own kind, he who made the tiniest flies as much more agile than great elephants as they are smaller; and though in the two the size of the limbs is unequal, yet the praise of the divine works is not unequal. For who that is of sound mind, and beholds the invisible things of God understood through the things that are made, would not praise God himself as craftsman in the little worm, whom he praises in the elephant? Or would not praise the same in the flea, whom he praises in the ox? Since even the figures which the skill of craftsmen is accustomed to form on gems the mind is wont to praise the more, the tinier they are that the eye beholds.

54. It must therefore be confessed that God created all things. But as for those things by which, at the divine nod, human transgression is beaten, when it is asked whether they were created by God before Adam sinned or after he sinned, the fitting answer is that those which are begotten either from the waters or from the earth were established in the beginning by God's creating at that time, by that Creator, indeed, who not only knew the nature of the man whom he was making, but also wonderfully foreknew that the man himself would sin. Nor did he make them in such a way that man before sin would either feel them as harmful or fear them. For no act of any earthly living creature could harm him, just as he had himself been established by divine gift as lord of them all. So it was the transgression of man himself, not the Creator's making, that made these things harmful and destructive to man. For it was not the kindness of the one creating that brought this about, but the justice of the one judging.

55. But those things which we see arise from the corruption of flesh or of fruits, we do not say came into being then, when in those six days God made all things very good; but those [things] were made in time in such a way that these would afterwards be born from them. To this corruption human flesh too was brought down, when, as it is written: Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. 48:13); so that now the necessity of corruption and death would hold the body of sinful man. From these two evils the bodies of the righteous are to be freed by the grace of God; not in this time, in which, just as God makes his sun rise on the good and the bad, and rains on the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), he not only caused the unbelieving Herod to be consumed by worms (Acts 12:23), but also permitted his servant Job to seethe with pus and worms (Job 2:8); but in the future the bodies of the righteous will feel no trouble of corruption and mortality, when in them this corruptible will put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53). In that life of the good and misery of the wicked, whatever there is for the good or for the wicked will be full and eternal. There comforts will not be mixed with torments, [nor torments] be set among comforts. There the eternity of joys and of punishments will remain without end; neither will the wicked hope for joys, nor the good fear sorrow: in the good there will always be abiding eternal exultation, but in the wicked weeping and gnashing of teeth will always remain; the company of demons will hold the unjust miserable for ever, but equality with the holy angels will receive the righteous, blessed for ever.

56. Accordingly, singing to God of mercy and judgement, let us not despise the time of mercy, so that we may come to judgement without fear. Let us hope in the judge whom we know as Redeemer. Let our works be such that everlasting rewards may be repaid for them. From the fact that we fear and avoid the troubles of the present time, we must consider how much we ought to flee eternal punishments. Let us turn away, then, from evil and do good: for every man will find in the time of divine retribution what he has had here in his works, as the Apostle says: For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap: for he who sows in his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption; but he who sows in the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life (Gal. 6:8). For this reason the same apostle admonishes us, saying: For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live (Rom. 8:13). Here, then, let us by the spirit put to death the deeds of the flesh, and, dead to sin, let us live to God. Let neither the prosperity of the world corrupt us nor its adversity break us. Let us move out in heart from the dwelling of this world, from which we are soon to move out in body too, so that that heavenly house may receive us, of which the Apostle says that we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor. 5:1). Of this it is written: Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you (Ps. 85:5). There, as the dwelling is eternal, so is the praising eternal. Those who dwell there always praise God, because they always exult over the Lord and in the Lord; and just as the eternity of the holy dwelling is sweet to those who praise, so the sweetness of praising is eternal for those who dwell [there].
